title: Lord Edward's covert crusade to Al-Karak reshapes Mediterranean power
hook: A forgotten feud turned a royal crusade into a covert power play in 1272.

beats.say: Edward, the young son of Henry III, was dispatched not for holy war but to rescue his sister's betrothed.
beats.visual: illustration of Edward I portrait medieval manuscript

beats.say: The target was the fortress of Al-Karak, where the Lusignan prince held a captive Armenian princess.
In secret, Edward hired Genoese mercenaries, promising them a share of the spice routes through the Levant.
The crusade fleet slipped past the Sicilian navy in October, exploiting a storm that scattered the papal fleet.
At Al-Karak, Edward's forces used Greek fire hidden in barrels, a technology rarely seen in the Holy Land.
The Lusignan prince fled, leaving behind a trove of Coptic manuscripts that revealed Byzantine diplomatic plans.
Edward seized the princess, marrying her to secure a claim over the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.
beats.visual: Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia map 13th century

beats.say: Returning to England, he leveraged the marriage to pressure the Pope into granting a new crusade charter.
Historians once called this a holy expedition, but archives show it was a calculated dynastic gamble.
The hidden agenda reshaped Mediterranean alliances, setting the stage for Edward's later campaigns in Wales and Scotland.
